This touches on a real ethical tension in couples therapy, and the answer depends on how the therapeutic relationship was set up from the start.

Many therapists who do both couples and individual work establish a "no secrets" policy up front, meaning information shared individually can be brought into couples sessions. Others hold confidentiality for individual sessions. Because of this risk of conflicting loyalties, many practitioners avoid seeing one partner individually while treating the couple. If confidentiality wasn't clarified beforehand, it becomes ethically complicated. Rather than forcing disclosure, a common approach is to work with the person who disclosed—helping them understand how the secret affects the therapy and encouraging them to share it themselves, while being clear that you can't do effective couples work around a hidden issue.

If you're facing this as a clinician, consulting your professional ethics code and a supervisor or peer consultation would be genuinely valuable here. If you're navigating this as someone in counseling, raising your concerns directly with your therapist is worthwhile.
